name: 3-5 Years Away Pattern
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Always Almost There: The Three-to-Five-Year Horizon
lesson.summary: A specific, recurring claim threads through quantum computing's history, that practical, fault-tolerant quantum computers are three to five years away, a horizon that has been restated at nearly every major milestone since the 1990s without ever arriving on schedule.
lesson.body:
If you read predictions about quantum computing made across different decades, one phrase recurs with almost comic regularity: useful quantum computers are three to five years away. This specific horizon shows up in research funding proposals from the 1990s, in D-Wave's marketing language around its 2007 launch, in commentary following Google's 2019 supremacy claim, and in roadmap slides accompanying IBM's chip announcements through 2023. The timeline pattern analysis in the previous chapter identified the broader phenomenon of shifting goalposts; this chapter isolates the specific number that keeps getting used, and asks why three to five years in particular is such a durable choice.

Three to five years is, not coincidentally, close to the outer edge of what most funders, investors, and corporate planning cycles are willing to underwrite without demanding results. It is short enough to justify continued investment now, since the payoff feels near, but long enough that the person making the prediction is rarely still in the same role when the deadline arrives and needs to be explained. A venture capital fund typically has a ten-year horizon, and a three-to-five-year prediction fits comfortably within an early or middle round without requiring proof by exit. A government grant cycle often runs three to five years, which means the prediction conveniently matches the length of the funding it justifies.

There is also a genuine cognitive reason this keeps happening, separate from any strategic incentive. Researchers working on the hardest remaining problem in front of them tend to underestimate how many additional hard problems are waiting behind it. Solving qubit coherence at small scale looks, from the inside, like the last major obstacle before scaling up, until it is solved, revealing the next obstacle, which then looks like the new last major obstacle. This is sometimes called the last-mile illusion, and it is not unique to quantum computing; it shows up in self-driving car predictions, nuclear fusion predictions, and general artificial intelligence predictions, all of which have their own version of the perpetually five-year-away breakthrough.

Applying this specifically to the milestones already covered: Google's 2019 Sycamore claim was followed by predictions that practical quantum advantage for real-world problems would follow within roughly five years, putting the target around 2024. IBM's Condor chip in 2023 came with roadmap language suggesting error-corrected, commercially useful systems within a similar window. Neither prediction was met on schedule, which is exactly what the zero-ROI finding for 2025 already demonstrated. The pattern is not that these predictions are always wrong forever, but that the same window keeps getting quoted at each new milestone rather than the window measurably shrinking as the field gets closer.

The practical takeaway for a skeptical reader is not to dismiss every three-to-five-year claim automatically, since eventually one of them will turn out to be roughly correct simply because the underlying engineering is real and does keep advancing. The useful move instead is to track whether a given three-to-five-year prediction comes with a specific, falsifiable technical milestone attached, such as a stated number of logical error-corrected qubits or a named algorithm running at a specified problem size, rather than a vague promise of usefulness. Predictions with concrete, checkable commitments are far rarer, and far more informative, than the recurring horizon number by itself.
